title: When the Machine Turns
premise: Freya Sandoval tends the Verdance, a terraformed garden orbiting a dead colony world, and maintains its beacon — a signal she discovers was never authorized by any government. When a name appears on the manifest of a ship that never flew, she learns the beacon is a fabrication: a lie broadcast for thirty years to keep two hostile fleets believing the colony survived and a peace treaty holds. As investigators from both fleets converge on the garden, Freya must decide whether to preserve the comforting lie or expose the truth, knowing either choice could ignite a war. In the end she forges a third path: she rewrites the beacon's message into an honest confession and invitation, forcing both fleets to meet in her garden and negotiate justice openly rather than through inherited deception.
about_author: Isandro Amberdale is the pen name of a former orbital systems engineer who spent six years writing technical documentation for life-support arrays before turning to fiction. They write slow-burning science fiction about people who maintain things — beacons, gardens, lies — long after everyone else has stopped caring whether those things are true.

chapters.title: The Garden of Unborn Seasons
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She walks the Verdance's terraces, pruning trees that will outlive her, and logs her daily beacon check with ritual calm. Small anomalies nag at her: maintenance requests routed to dead departments, a manifest terminal that boots to a ship designation she doesn't recognize. The emotional beat is quiet loneliness — devotion without witness — ending when she finds one new name on the never-flown ship's crew list.

chapters.title: A Name That Was Never Signed
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The name — Elin Marchetti — matches no birth registry in either fleet's archives. Digging through the station's sealed records, Freya finds the beacon's original commissioning order is unsigned, dated three years after the colony was declared lost. Her wonder curdles into unease; someone built this lie deliberately, and now something inside it has changed.

chapters.title: Two Fleets, One Silence
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Freya and Commander Dae-Ho Yun of the Meridian Fleet, whose long-range sensors detect the beacon flickering off-pattern for eleven seconds. Yun is ordered to investigate quietly; his rival, Captain Soraya Venn of the Concordance, receives the same order. The beat is dread: two armed ships converging on a garden tended by one woman who doesn't yet know she's the only thing keeping them apart.

chapters.title: What the Beacon Was For
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She breaches the beacon's physical core and finds handwritten letters from the original terraforming crew — confessions that the colony died in an accident both fleets caused and blamed on each other. The survivors built the beacon to impersonate a living colony so neither side would return to fight over the corpse. The beat is grief transformed into terrible understanding: her whole vocation is a monument to a cover-up.

chapters.title: Eleven Seconds
chapters.summary: Yun's POV. His shuttle docks at the Verdance under pretense of inspection. He is courteous, precise, and lying about everything. Freya plays the naive caretaker while cataloguing his questions, realizing he already suspects the truth. The beat is a duel of manners — two people performing innocence across a table of tea grown from seeds meant for children who were never born.

chapters.title: The Manifest Ghost
chapters.summary: Venn's POV, arriving unannounced. Venn is harsher, faster, and carries private orders to seize the beacon core as evidence of Meridian war crimes. She confronts Freya directly, and Freya makes a split-second choice: she claims the anomaly was her own unauthorized repair, buying time but making herself culpable in both fleets' eyes. The beat is fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Holding the Lie Together
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. With both commanders aboard and suspicious of each other, Freya improvises — forging maintenance logs, staging the garden's automated systems as evidence of a thriving colony, feeding each commander carefully different truths. It works, barely, but she realizes the lie now requires a liar full-time, and she is becoming the machine that turns. The beat is vertigo: power feels exactly like competence until it doesn't.

chapters.title: Elin Marchetti
chapters.summary: Yun's POV. Yun decrypts the manifest and discovers Elin Marchetti was a real person — a Concordance whistleblower who died exposing the accident, erased from every record by both sides. The 'new name' was the beacon's dying author leaving a confession timed to surface decades later. Yun must choose between his orders and the truth. The beat is moral awakening: the law he serves was built on the crime.

chapters.title: When the Machine Turns
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, climax. Venn attempts to seize the core; Yun blocks her; weapons arm in the garden Freya swore to protect. Freya broadcasts the beacon's full confession — the accident, the erasure, the thirty-year lie — to both fleets simultaneously, then shuts the machine down forever. The beat is catharsis through surrender: she destroys her life's work to make the truth undeniable.

chapters.title: Planting in Open Ground
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, months later. A joint tribunal convenes aboard the Verdance — justice outside any single fleet's law, held in the garden itself. The lie is gone; the fleets are angry, grieving, and talking. Freya plants a new terrace, this time labeled with real names, including Elin Marchetti's. The beat is hard-won hope: nothing is resolved cleanly, but everything is finally honest.
